One thing that always bothers me in fiction is that Elves/Space Elves/Eldar or whatever other long-lived races you have flying around usually are just pointy-eared humans with an arrogant and haughty personality. I know that they want the characters to be relatable and understandable to the average viewer, but realistically speaking, wouldn't a person whose life is measured in centuries or even millennia rather than decades have or at least develop a mindset completely alien when compared to that of a human?

I would expect you'd grow increasingly nihilistic and apathetic beyond a certain point. But then again, it's equally possible that such beings would hold themselves to a very strict code of conduct to avoid exactly that.
How do you think extreme longevity or outright immortality would affect the psyche of a humanoid character?

I think it would destroy it. A mind would end up so far removed from the herd that it would collapse in on itself. By the time a person is 70 years old they begin to question their own memories. Imagine if that person was 700 years old. They wouldn't be able to know if events they had witnessed were being portrayed correctly, and even if they did know for a certainty, how would they convince anyone that they were right and "history" was wrong?

I think most would become apathetic, which is generally how they are depicted. Even their haughty arrogance is really just them upset others are bothering them with shit that doesn't matter at all. All the mortals sound like teenagers complaining about how their life is over because of some petty garbage.

Progress would plummet. A huge part of our drive is to outshine the previous generations, if the previous generation never passes on the torch the more locked into the status quo we become.

In the end, boredom would be what destroyed us. A collective "hold my beer" self destructive time period. At least with a small percentage of the population but but enough to end it for everyone else. Ones with the mental disapline will match onto an impossible goal to always strive towards.

I think the only way humanity would survive immortality is if we went fully digital. Spending the time creating and living infinite gaming worlds.
Tolkien's Elves were generally sad BECAUSE of all the long years of sorrow they lived through. They weren't typically arrogant compared to others, except for Fëanor and his children.

I disagree with the presentation of such characters as nihilistic or apathetic. I don't care about the people around me because I'm going to die one day, I would have to be a psychopath to not care. Even if others lifespan were shorter. Talk to a guy who has owned ten dogs and ask whether he loves his dog. He may have a longer perspective but that doesn't mean he doesn't care.

A long lifespan would mostly provide an awareness of the very long term effects of a person's actions. If I do this now what will that mean in 300 years? It also allows a longer time, in human-like societies, to understand oneself, to overcome one's own flaws, and to build up wealth.

From a slightly positive aspect, with the benefit of centuries of life versus decades, you would be come more consciously aware of the patterns and cycles that emerge over the course of history. You can get an idea of it from studying history, but to fully grasp it would require living through it and experiencing it first hand. Since these cycles can often take decades or eveb centuries to repeat, you might only ever see a small piece of the bigger picture with the limited lifespan of an average human.

The downside is realizing that even if you see the patterns emerging, you will in all likelyhood be unable to do anything to stop them, or alter the outcome to a more positive end. And who is to say you should even try? Being aware of the patterns could be entirely destructive, or very useful in bettering your existence depending on how you use the knowledge.

The benefits of immortality largely come down to a personal level. If you spend the time constantly improving your skillset, your knowledge, and your abilities, then it can be a great thing.

This all assumes, of course, that your brain has adapted and adjusted to the stress of living forever, and it's not simplya baseline human brain jammed into an immortal body.
